title: Ananda weeps
hook: Ananda weeps outside; the Buddha praises him as the kindest attendant

segments.voice: Yesterday: four places that stir the heart, and your line, four places. Which place in your life did you slow down for? Today the man who asked about those places slips away and cries. Day five hundred fifty.

Hospitals have a particular hallway. The one just outside the room, where family members go to fall apart for a minute so they can walk back in steady. Ananda has served the Buddha for many years: fetching water, guarding the door, remembering every word. Now, at Kusinara, he goes into a dwelling, leans against the door frame, and weeps. I'm still a learner, he says. I still have work to do. And my teacher, who was so kind to me, is about to pass away. The Buddha notices he's gone and asks the monks: where is Ananda? Today: Ananda weeps.
screen: `THE HALLWAY OUTSIDE THE ROOM.` → `LEANING ON THE DOOR FRAME.` → `WHERE IS ANANDA?`

segments.voice: He sends a monk: go and tell Ananda the teacher is calling him. Ananda comes back, bows, and sits to one side. And the Buddha doesn't tell him to stop crying. He says: enough, Ananda. Don't grieve. Haven't I told you that we must be parted from everything dear to us? How could anything born, put together, bound to fall apart, not fall apart? Then he turns and thanks him. For a long time, Ananda, you've attended on me with kindness in body, in speech and in mind, helpfully, gladly, wholeheartedly, without measure. You've done well. Keep at it, and you'll soon be free. Then he speaks to all the monks about Ananda, in praise. The Buddhas of the past had attendants as good as Ananda, he says, and so will those of the future. Ananda is wise. He knows the right time for monks, nuns, lay followers, kings and teachers of other schools to come and see me. And he names something wonderful about him, true for monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen alike. When any of them come to see Ananda, they're glad just to see him. When he speaks, they're glad to hear him. And when he stops, they wish he'd go on. Picture it. In his last hours, the Buddha spends real time making sure everyone in the room knows how good this man has been. Later tradition says Ananda reached awakening just before the first great council, so that he could recite the discourses there, which is why so many of them begin, thus have I heard.
screen: `DON'T GRIEVE: ALL THAT'S DEAR CHANGES.` · `KINDNESS IN BODY, SPEECH AND MIND.` · `PRAISED IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` · `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` · then, large: `YOU'VE DONE WELL, ANANDA.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone who has helped you faithfully. A parent, a nurse, a colleague, a friend who drives you to the airport. Picture their face. Let three things come up: something kind they did, something kind they said, something kind they must have wished for you. Stay with each for a few breaths. Then, quietly, let the Buddha's line form for them: you've done well. The bell holds the time.
Ananda weeps. At Kusinara the attendant cries in a doorway; the Buddha calls him back, comforts him, and praises his years of kindness. Today's word.
Your line: you've done well, Ananda. Today, thank one person who has helped you faithfully, by name, and tell them exactly what they did. Day five hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions honor Ananda as the disciple who remembered and recited the discourses, and the phrase 'thus have I heard' that opens many suttas is traditionally understood as his voice.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha, near the end. your attendant has slipped out to cry. what do you do?
options: send for him, comfort him, and praise his service in front of everyone.
tell the others not to grieve like him.
fork.reveal: he calls Ananda back, comforts him, thanks him, and praises him to all the monks.

original.note: Pali Ananda: joy, delight. the name of the attendant who wept.

trapdoor: what you thought: an awakened teacher would be above someone else's tears.
what it means: the Buddha comforts Ananda, reminds him of change, and spends his last hours praising him.
what a scholar hears: DN 16 lists four acchariya abbhuta dhamma of Ananda; the Cullavagga's account of the first council places his arahantship on the eve of the council.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), Ananda weeps and is praised

notes: DN 16 paraphrased. Confirm: Ananda leans on the door-post (kapisisa) and weeps; the Buddha's comfort; the praise of service in body, speech and mind; the four wonderful qualities.
Ananda's awakening just before the first council follows the Cullavagga; the script says 'later tradition says'.
'Thus have I heard' as Ananda's voice is the traditional understanding; confirm framing.
